title: Consolidated rollout forensics and telemetry-poisoning playbook
creator: Aisha Raman
description: Summary: After a recent staged model rollout that produced subtle degradations in a subset of customers, we discovered noisy and misleading telemetry signals that delayed automated rollback. This ticket consolidates the postmortem findings into a reproducible forensic checklist, implements a lightweight detector for telemetry poisoning (i.e., synthetic or outlier signal injection from canary traffic), and codifies a playbook that ties detection thresholds to auto-rollback and human validation gates. Goals: 1) Reduce time-to-rollback for rollout failures caused or masked by telemetry anomalies; 2) Make runbooks reproducible and searchable; 3) Add automated sanity checks that prevent metric poisoning from suppressing safety gates.
acceptance_criteria: A forensic checklist (confluence doc) exists with step-by-step triage for canary/AB/shadow failures
A telemetry-poisoning detector (lightweight rule-based) runs in the canary pipeline and flags suspicious signal patterns
Auto-rollback policy is updated to require a secondary validated signal when detector fires, with a clear human-in-loop path
At least two historical incidents were replayed through the new detector to validate true-positive behavior and low false-positive rate
Runbook includes sample CLI commands, relevant dashboards, and links to artifacts (PRs, logs, model manifests)
steps_taken: Collected telemetry from the failed rollout (timestamped metrics, traces, model outputs, KV-cache keys) and stored artifacts in gs://redwood-postmortems/2025-02-canary-fail
Ran a correlation analysis between increased latency spikes and sudden shifts in per-token entropy and discovered two customer-specific query patterns that generated atypical prefix caching behavior
Identified that the canary traffic generator replay used synthetic prompts with repeated token sequences that caused cache key collisions and misleading success metrics

Built a small rule-set to detect: (a) sudden burst of identical KV cache keys; (b) divergence between synthetic and production response distributions (token entropy + length); (c) mismatch between request ID churn and expected traffic mix
Piloted the detector against three previous rollout incidents (ENG-29901, ENG-341219, ENG-7124) and logged results in the forensic workspace
decisions: Ship a rule-based detector first (fast iteration) and postpone an ML classifier until we have more labeled incidents
Require the detector to be consensus-aware: it must see multiple signals (cache collision + response divergence) before suppressing auto-rollback
Add a mandatory manual verification step (oncall ack) for any detector suppression that lasts longer than 15 minutes
Centralize telemetry poisoning findings under a searchable Confluence page and tag incidents for future classifier training
risks: False positives from the detector could cause unnecessary rollbacks if thresholds are too aggressive
Detector may not generalize across model families and quantization profiles without additional tuning
Inadequate historical labeling could delay ML classifier development
Operator burden: oncall may receive more alerts if UI/triage flows are not improved
